                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive training may enhance cognition and support brain health during aging, but few trials have evaluated readily accessible chatbot-based programs with neuroimaging outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a chatbot-based cognitive training program on white matter microstructural organization and cognition in cognitively unimpaired older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a single-blind randomized controlled trial, 72 cognitively unimpaired older adults were assigned to chatbot-based cognitive training (30 min/day, 5 days/week for 12 weeks; n=37) or a no-intervention control (n=35). Diffusion tensor imaging at baseline and 12 weeks quantified fractional anisotropy (FA) in predefined white matter tracts, and cognition was assessed with the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Groups were comparable at baseline. After 12 weeks, the training group showed significantly less FA reduction than controls in the bilateral tapetum and right posterior thalamic radiation, surviving false discovery rate control (P<.05). The training group also improved on Paired Associates Learning (PAL), an episodic memory measure (P=.04). PAL improvement was positively associated with FA change in the right posterior thalamic radiation and right sagittal stratum (false discovery rate–adjusted P=.04 for each).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that a 12-week chatbot-based cognitive training program may support episodic memory and the relative maintenance of white matter microstructural organization in selected pathways in cognitively unimpaired older adults, consistent with a brain-maintenance framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial Registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CRIS KCT0004630; https://tinyurl.com/4xfesb68</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Impact of Chatbot-Based Cognitive Training on Cognitive Function and White Matter Integrity in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults: Randomized Controlled Trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Technology-based rehabilitation is increasingly used for balance training in older adults. A 2023 network meta-analysis (NMA) found only exergaming with motion capture superior to no treatment; however, the evidence has since expanded, and no GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) appraisal has been applied.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to update the comparative effectiveness of 5 technology categories—exergaming with balance platforms (EBP), exergaming with motion capture (EMC), other serious games, interventions with wearables, and telerehabilitation (Tele)—versus conventional exercise (CE), and no treatment (NT), applying GRADE adapted for NMA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic search of 4 databases from inception through April 2025, with an identical supplementary update search to January 31, 2026, identified 60 randomized controlled trials (N=3469; mean age 73.1, SD 5.2; range 63.3-86.2 y). Fifty-seven trials (2758 analyzed participants) contributed to 4 prespecified networks (all balance, functional scales, Timed Up and Go [TUG] test, and gait speed). A random-effects NMA was fitted using multivariate meta-regression. Treatment hierarchies were summarized by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) and the probability of being best; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE adapted for NMA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the all-balance network, Tele (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.69, 95% CI 0.08‐1.29;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), EBP (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.31‐0.95;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), EMC (SMD 0.58, 95% CI 0.22‐0.95;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.002), and CE (SMD 0.35, 95% CI 0.03‐0.68;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03) were superior to NT, with consistent findings in the TUG network (EBP 0.81, 95% CI 0.42‐1.20; Tele 0.82, 95% CI 0.16‐1.49; EMC 0.79, 95% CI 0.36‐1.21; all
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.05). Tele ranked first by SUCRA (76.3%), but its probability of being best was only approximately 41%, and the estimate rested on 5 trials (n=198). No technology-based intervention was superior to CE in any network. Certainty of evidence was moderate for EBP versus NT and EMC versus NT in the TUG network only; the 37 other comparisons were low or very low. Dropout did not differ between technology-based and control arms (odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.87‐1.40;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.41).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Tele, EBP, and EMC were each associated with improved balance versus NT, although none exceeded CE. The first-place SUCRA ranking of Tele is preliminary. Certainty was moderate only for EBP and EMC versus NT on the TUG test; the remaining evidence is too uncertain for firm clinical recommendations. As no included trial reported falls, these findings are not direct evidence of fall prevention. Larger trials with standardized comparator intensity and posttraining follow-up are required.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Comparative Effectiveness of Digital Exercise-Based Interventions for Improving Balance in Older Adults: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis With GRADE Certainty of Evidence

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Delirium is common among older adults, particularly those with cognitive impairment. However, delirium among patients with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in long-term care (LTC) hospitals has received limited attention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine delirium occurrence and associated factors among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 142 patients aged 65 years or older with dementia (n=100, 70.4%) or MCI (n=42, 29.6%) at 2 LTC hospitals in South Korea between September 2021 and August 2022. Delirium occurrence was defined as at least 1 positive Short Confusion Assessment Method assessment during twice-daily assessments over 4 weeks, including the first assessment. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors overall and within each cognitive group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Delirium was identified in 55 (38.7%) of 142 patients. The proportion was 41% (41/100) in patients with dementia and 33.3% (14/42) in patients with MCI. Hypoactive delirium was the most common subtype (33/55, 60%). Overall, female sex (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.344, 95% CI 1.794-10.515; P=.001), immobility (aOR 4.953, 95% CI 1.857-13.205; P=.001), and analgesic use (aOR 3.641, 95% CI 1.262-10.501; P=.02) were associated with delirium. Infection was inversely associated with delirium (aOR 0.251, 95% CI 0.101-0.623; P=.003). In patients with dementia, female sex, immobility, analgesic use, and pain were associated with delirium. Diaper use was associated with delirium in patients with MCI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Delirium was common among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals. The findings support regular delirium assessment, with attention to mobility and pain-related care needs. Further studies are needed to clarify the factors associated with delirium in each cognitive group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Delirium Occurrence and Associated Factors Among Patients With Dementia and Mild Cognitive Impairment Admitted to Long-Term Care Hospitals: Cross-Sectional Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High-resolution digital cognitive tools administered at frequent intervals enable the study of age-related cognitive change at a previously unattainable level of granularity. Computational modeling further enables the simultaneous examination of multiple aspects of cognitive performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The objective of this study was to examine whether repeated digital multiday learning assessments can detect age-related cognitive decline over short time frames in cognitively unimpaired older adults and to quantify age-related differences in process-based cognitive markers derived from computational modeling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 209 cognitively unimpaired older adults (mean age 73.6, SD 8.2 years; n=136, 65.1% female) from the Harvard Aging Brain Study and affiliated studies were administered the Boston Remote Assessment for Neurocognitive Health, which includes the face-name task, a paired associative learning task. Daily median response times for correct responses were used as the primary outcome. A new version of the face-name task was administered across up to 4 testing intervals over a mean of 2.8 (SD 0.4) years. Using computational modeling, we estimated longitudinal changes in peak performance, a practice-adjusted marker of an individual’s best expected response time, as an indicator of age-related cognitive decline. We further examined age-related differences in peak performance, stability (within-person variability), learning within and across testing intervals, and between-interval forgetting, with embedded linear regressions for age, sex, years of education, and device type.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Peak performance slowed by 0.04 seconds per year (95% credible interval 0.02-0.06; approximately 2% per year), indicating age-related cognitive decline. Higher age (+1-SD) was associated with slower peak performance (+0.19 seconds, 95% credible interval 0.12-0.26), steeper annual slowing in peak performance (+0.036 seconds per year), greater within-person variability (+0.043 seconds), reduced learning across testing intervals, and more forgetting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings indicate that a digital multiday learning paradigm combined with computational modeling of response times sensitively detects age-related cognitive decline over short timescales (<3 years), which are difficult to capture in conventional study designs relying on infrequent assessments. In addition, this approach identifies specific process-based cognitive markers associated with aging, including slower performance, reduced stability, and diminished learning across testing intervals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Detection of Age-Related Cognitive Decline Over Short Time Frames Using Digital Multiday Learning Assessments: Longitudinal Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Telemonitoring offers solutions for remote health management among older adults; yet, acceptance varies based on individual perceptions and presentation strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This 2-phased sequential mixed methods study examines the role of message framing on telemonitoring adoption among low-income older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Phase 1 involved in-depth interviews with 17 older adults, identifying key facilitators (accessibility, affordability, and health benefits) and barriers (preference for in-person consultations, technological limitations, and information processing difficulties) of telemonitoring. Building on these insights, phase 2 used an experimental study with 120 participants assessing message framing effects (episodic vs thematic) and modalities (video vs photo-text) on telemonitoring adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Episodic framing did not produce a significant main effect on attitudes toward telemonitoring; however, its effect was moderated by external locus of control (LOC), with episodic framing associated with more positive attitudes among participants lower in external LOC, and thematic framing more favorable among those higher in external LOC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Convenience, cost, and health benefits emerged as key adoption drivers, while traditional consultation preferences and cognitive processing challenges posed barriers. Theoretical and practical implications were discussed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Telemonitoring Adoption Among Older Adults: Sequential Mixed Methods Study of Message Framing and Structural Influence

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment requires preserving physical, cognitive, and psychosocial functioning to sustain their independence and quality of life. However, existing interventions vary in design, delivery format, and composition, and evidence regarding their effectiveness across these three core domains remains inconsistent. This study aimed to identify the most effective intervention types for specific domains of healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five electronic databases were searched for studies published from October 2015 to June 2026. Randomized controlled trials reporting at least two outcomes—among physical capability, cognitive function, or psychosocial well-being—were reviewed. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 tool. A dependency-aware multilevel random-effects meta-analysis with trial-clustered robust inference was conducted in R, supplemented by moderator tests, prediction intervals, sensitivity analyses, reporting-bias assessments, and GRADE evaluations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multicomponent interventions were associated with beneficial effects on cognitive and psychosocial outcomes, whereas group-based interventions showed beneficial effects across all three domains and a significantly greater effect on cognitive function than individually delivered interventions. Despite substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals, these findings were generally robust across sensitivity analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The observed advantages of group-based delivery, particularly for cognitive function, and multicomponent approaches for cognitive and psychosocial outcomes highlight the domain-specific nature of intervention effects. These findings support tailoring intervention delivery and component configuration to the targeted domain rather than applying a uniform approach to healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Intervention-Type-Specific Effects on Healthy Aging of Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Extreme climate events can threaten older adults’ health. The purpose of this study was to summarize existing literature on older adults’ climate health literacy, defined as their ability to find and access, understand, and act upon information related to climate-related health threats.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scoping review was conducted in the bibliographic databases Embase, Medline and Scopus and grey literature sources Cornell Initiative for Research on Climate and Aging and Climate Change and Human Health Literature portals with searches updated January 2026. English language studies of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years and older were included if they reported at least one aspect of climate health literacy. Quantitative data were reported as median percentages, and qualitative themes were categorized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifty-nine studies, including 22,992 records for 20,296 unique participants, were included. Most recognized the health risks of extreme climate events but did not identify personal vulnerability. Television was the most cited source of information and hydration, clothing and environment modification, and activity adjustment were the most utilized adaptive actions. Barriers to adaptive actions included financial constraints, limited mobility and lack of supports. The effectiveness of studied interventions was mixed, influenced by intervention type and study design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite access to information and awareness of climate-related health threats, gaps remain in personal risk perception and translation of knowledge into actions. Improving climate health literacy among older adults requires public health messaging, engagement of trustworthy authorities, and interventions addressing social and structural barriers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Perceptions, Knowledge, and Adaptive actions in Response to Climate Events: A Scoping Review of Climate Health Literacy among Community Dwelling Older Adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The global aging population has led to an increasing number of older active drivers. While age-related physical and cognitive changes are associated with increased crash risk, specific on-road adaptations and safety outcomes of older drivers remain unclear. This study examined distinct driving characteristics, personality traits, and cognitive processes related to decision-making among middle-aged and older drivers in a simulated driving environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We assessed driving performance in a high-fidelity motorcycle simulator across drivers in three age groups: middle-aged (30-54; n = 40), aged 65–74 (n = 34), and aged 75 + (75-86; n = 29). Comparative analysis focused on speed regulation, braking behavior, control stability, and accident rates. Additionally, questionnaire measures and a computerized decision-making task were employed to assess risk perception and risky decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared to the middle-aged group, both older groups demonstrated a significantly more conservative driving profile: lower mean speeds, fewer speeding violations, longer braking maneuvers, reduced variation in throttle control, and a lower incidence of simulated accidents. Drivers aged 75+ also reported higher perceived risk in driving scenarios and displayed diminished discrimination between risk and non-risk situations in a braking decision task. Mediation analyses showed that steering variance in the simulator and self-reported health/safety risk-taking significantly mediated the relationship between age group and number of accidents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that older drivers adopt proactive compensatory strategies that could result in fewer simulated accidents. These findings challenge a purely deficit-oriented perspective on older driver safety, underscoring the critical role of behavioral adaptation and strategic self-regulation in maintaining safe mobility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Adaptive driving, not unsafe: Older drivers’ compensatory strategies and lower simulated crash risk

records.abstract: <jats:p>Knowledge of dementia facilitates early detection, care planning, and stigma reduction, yet less is known about dementia knowledge among Asian American populations. This study examined correlates of dementia knowledge among 505 Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese Americans aged 50 and older residing in Central Florida. Dementia knowledge was assessed using the Dementia Knowledge Assessment Scale with four subscales. Linear regression analyses examined associations of dementia knowledge with sociodemographic, immigration, social, digital and information, and dementia experiences and attitudinal factors. Participants demonstrated low overall dementia knowledge. Digital literacy was positively associated with total dementia knowledge and all subscales except communication and behavior. Limited English proficiency was negatively associated with knowledge in the causes and characteristics subscale. The perceived importance of dementia planning was positively associated with total dementia knowledge and three subscales. Subscale-specific findings should be interpreted cautiously because of varying subscale reliability, particularly for communication and behavior.</jats:p>
title: Dementia Knowledge Among Older Asian Americans: Roles of Digital Literacy, Planning Attitudes, and Sociocultural Contexts

records.abstract: <jats:p>More than 60% of older workers report experiencing ageism in the workplace, yet little is known about whether the relationship between ageism, job satisfaction, and mental health differs by US-born status. This study examined whether job satisfaction mediates the association between workplace ageism and depressive symptoms and assessed whether this association differs by US-born status. Data were drawn from the 2018 and 2020 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 for workers aged 53- 62, and a multiple-group path analysis was conducted. The results indicated that, among US-born workers, job satisfaction significantly mediated the associations between depressive symptoms and both ageism in promotion and ageism in early retirement. Among immigrant workers, however, this mediating effect was significant only for ageism in promotion. Findings underscore the importance of developing anti-ageism policies that adopt an intersectional approach, jointly considering US-born status and age to reduce the detrimental impacts of ageism on workers’ mental health.</jats:p>
title: Workplace Ageism, Job Satisfaction, and Depressive Symptoms Among Older Workers: The Roles of US-Born Status

records.abstract: <jats:p>As populations age and the share of retirees increases across Europe, the question of whether individuals stay active after retirement is increasingly salient. Retirees are known to provide more instrumental support than their working counterparts. However, most previous studies have relied on between-group comparisons of retirees and employed individuals, leaving it unclear how the transition into retirement affects changes in instrumental support within individuals over time. Using eight waves of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe covering 19 countries between 2004–2022 (n = 7,422 observations from 3,711 individuals aged 50+), we employed fixed-effects regression and found that the transition from employment to retirement was associated with an increase in instrumental support provision outside the household. We also found suggestive evidence that this association was stronger in countries with higher social expenditures. These findings indicate that retirement may promote activity and facilitate engagement in helping others.</jats:p>
title: Changes in Instrumental Support Around Retirement: Longitudinal Evidence From Europe

records.abstract: <jats:p>Older adults who need community services may remain uncertain whether those services are locally provided or judge that they are not. Research on perceived unmet need often combines these positions. Using a cross-sectional survey of 929 adults aged 60 or older in urban Jiangsu, China, we paired reported need with perceived provision across 20 services and distinguished awareness gaps, perceived non-provision, and comparison uncertainty for services not reported as needed. Fractional logit models examined associations with social participation and functional status. Greater social participation was associated with fewer awareness gaps, concentrated among adults with ADL disability (−8.75 percentage points per SD). A weaker, less stable association with perceived non-provision appeared among functionally independent adults, and no counterpart appeared for comparison uncertainty. Unresolved uncertainty and negative provision judgments may call for different responses, and outreach may be especially relevant for older adults with ADL disability.</jats:p>
title: Need-Conditioned Uncertainty and Perceived Non-Provision of Community Services: Social Participation and Functional Status Among Older Adults in Urban China

records.abstract: <jats:p>Person-centered care (PCC) is the gold standard for improving the quality of life (QoL) of people living with dementia. The Montessori method represents a practical model for implementing PCC in Nursing Homes (NHs). To date, no study has documented how residents describe their QoL in NHs implementing this method using a self-report approach consistent with PCC principles. This study explores residents’ perceptions of their QoL, as well as how they relate it to the care model, using a qualitative self-assessment tool. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty-nine residents from two NHs with high levels of Montessori implementation assessed using a validated tool. All interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three interconnected themes emerged. The first examines the components of QoL that matter most to residents. The second explores how the care model influences these determinants. Finally, the third describes residents’ self-assessment of QoL shaped by individual factors. Our study contributes to a better understanding of the Montessori method as a comprehensive PCC model from residents’ perspectives and deepens knowledge of the extent to which it can shape their QoL. These findings also provide practical and methodological insights for evaluating QoL and guiding care models promoting QoL.</jats:p>
title: Exploring Quality of Life Through Residents’ Voice in Nursing Homes: A Qualitative Study of a Montessori-Based Person-Centered Model of Care

records.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose: People with dementia can and do live successfully on their own, but there are additional challenges for people living alone without informal support. This paper reports findings of the first study in the UK to examine needs and experiences of, and services for, people with dementia who live alone without informal support. Method: The study involved a service audit of 13 local authority commissioners in two English regions, interviews with 22 people with dementia who live alone without informal carers, and case studies of four services supporting this group. Findings: Awareness of this population among commissioners was limited. There were very few services which explicitly supported this group, and some mainstream services excluded people without carers. None of the local authorities collected data on numbers of people with dementia living alone, or those without informal support, in their area. Some participants with dementia had contacted social care, but this had not always resulted in appropriate support, and people reported problematic interactions with staff, assumptions that friends would provide care, and support not being available at the right time. Self-funders were left with little support. People with dementia were resourceful, using general services, technology, and other tactics, including cleaners, meal delivery, community taxis, and automatic reminders to organise their lives. However, as many of these additional services have a cost attached, there is potential to exacerbate existing inequalities. Participants wanted more support, particularly with finances and administrative tasks. Services can help this group with supported handovers, allowing self-referral back into a service, and keeping case files open. Conclusions: Both the number of people with dementia, and the number of people ageing without children, are rising, and it will therefore become increasingly important to facilitate effective support for people with dementia to live independently without informal support.</jats:p>
title: Living Alone With Dementia: Managing Without Informal Support to Contact and Navigate Services

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Extreme heat is a major environmental threat to healthy ageing, with older people experiencing the highest rates of heat-related morbidity and mortality. Although age-related physiological changes, multimorbidity and frailty remain key determinants of heat susceptibility, climate change, social inequalities and energy insecurity are reshaping the conditions in which older people experience and respond to thermal stress. This narrative New Horizons review integrates evidence identified through a structured, non-systematic search of peer-reviewed literature and relevant institutional reports across geriatric medicine, environmental health and climate science. It examines how frailty, intrinsic capacity, housing, energy affordability and social frailty influence the ability of older people to recognise risk, access protection and respond effectively to extreme heat. Particular attention is given to energy insecurity and summer cooling poverty, through which limited access to affordable household energy may undermine resilience. Ageing models primarily characterise individual vulnerability and functioning within the environment, whereas climate vulnerability models organise risk around exposure, sensitivity and adaptation; we use adaptive capacity to connect these perspectives by asking whether personal and contextual resources can be mobilised for protection. It may provide a conceptual basis for developing and subsequently validating a heat-adapted comprehensive geriatric assessment and for informing targeted prevention and climate adaptation policies for ageing populations.</jats:p>
title: New horizons in adaptive capacity and heat-related health in older people: integrating frailty, energy insecurity and social resources

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common disorder among elderly patients undergoing surgery and is associated with a higher risk of adverse outcomes. This meta-analysis investigated the effects of esketamine on postoperative sleep quality among elderly patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PubMed, Embase, The Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang databases were searched to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous esketamine with control in elderly patients (≥ 60 years) undergoing elective surgery in general anesthesia. Sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1 was the primary outcome. Other outcomes included sleep quality at other time points, objective sleep parameters, pain, cognitive function, and adverse events.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventeen RCTs involving 2587 patients were included. Regarding the primary outcome, esketamine significantly improved subjective sleep quality on POD 1 (SMD = -0.72; 95% CI, -1.10 to -0.34; I² = 93%), POD 2 (SMD = -1.40; 95% CI, -2.15 to -0.64; I² = 97%), and POD 7 (SMD = -0.38; 95% CI, -0.62 to -0.14; I² = 53%). Objective sleep measures on POD 1 revealed longer total sleep time, reduced sleep latency, and improved sleep efficiency. Esketamine also decreased pain intensity (SMD = -0.63; 95% CI, -0.88 to -0.38; I² = 70%) and improved MMSE scores (SMD = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.42 to 0.89; I² = 0%). Esketamine was associated with a lower risk of nausea or vomiting. No significant differences was observed between the two groups in terms of dizziness, while hypotension occurred less frequently with esketamine.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among elderly surgical patients, perioperative esketamine was associated with improved postoperative sleep quality, reduced pain intensity, and a potential improvement in cognitive function, without a significant increase in the risk of major adverse events. However, high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and determine optimal dosing regimens. Of note, all 17 included trials were conducted in China, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings to other populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Effects of esketamine on postoperative sleep quality in elderly patients under general anesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Traumatic cholecystitis after hip fracture is rare, but its prognosis is poor. However, studies that explore the risk factors for traumatic cholecystitis in older patients with hip fractures and establish effective predictive models were limited. Therefore, our study focused on the following three questions: (1)What were the characteristics of traumatic cholecystitis in older hip fracture patients? (2) What were the risk factors for traumatic cholecystitis in older hip fracture patients? (3) What was the best model for predicting traumatic cholecystitis in older hip fracture patients and analyze it globally and locally interpretatively using SHAP values?</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We retrospectively collected all clinical parameters of older hip fracture patients admitted to the Third Hospital of Hebei Medical University from January 2018 to December 2022. We developed five machine learning models for traumatic cholecystitis, which included logistic regression model(LR), random forest model(RF), lightGBM, XGBoost and KNN. We evaluate the predictive performance and clinical applicability of the LR model using the area under the ROC curve, calibration curve, and clinical decision curve. We evaluated the machine learning models by calculating AUC-ROC, PR-AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1 score. SHAP values were used to interpret the models, enhancing clinicians’ understanding and application of the models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study included 2376 patients, with an incidence rate of traumatic cholecystitis of 1.3% (30/2376). Independent risk factors for traumatic cholecystitis in older hip fracture patients included the C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR), history of biliary disease, haemoglobin (HB), albumin, hypokalaemia, and CRP. RF showed the highest PR-AUC (0.940, 95% CI: 0.835–0.997) among the five models. The ROC-AUC for the five models were 0.999(95% CI: 0.998,1.000) (RF), 0.741(95% CI: 0.649,0.839) (XGBoost), 0.852(95% CI: 0.785,0.915) (LR), 0.971(95% CI: 0.955,0.984) (LightGBM), and 0.980(95% CI: 0.975,0.985) (KNN), with sensitivities ranging from 26.7% (LR) to 100% (RF). The accuracy of these models ranged from 91.8%% (LightGBM) to 99.7% (RF). The random forest model performed the best.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among the five machine learning models, the random forest model showed the best discriminative performance in the present dataset, but this exploratory finding may overestimate its true predictive capability because of the small number of positive cases and lack of external validation. SHAP values were used to improve model interpretability. In the absence of large-scale prospective validation, this random forest algorithm can serve as an auxiliary perioperative comprehensive risk stratification tool, helping clinicians identify potential high-risk older patients as early as possible and implement closer monitoring of abdominal signs.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>This study explores how the service use and paid care costs of people with mild-to-moderate dementia in Britain change over a 7-year period, and which demographic and health characteristics were associated with variations in costs.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Frailty is a major determinant of adverse health outcomes in older adults, yet evidence comparing commonly used frailty instruments in patients hospitalized with infectious diseases is limited. We aimed to compare the prognostic performance of the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and the FRAIL Scale for predicting short-term outcomes in older adults admitted to infectious diseases departments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This prospective multicentre observational cohort study included adults aged ≥ 65 years hospitalized in infectious diseases departments across 16 hospitals in Türkiye. Frailty was rated at enrolment, during acute illness, using the CFS (frail: ≥5) and the FRAIL Scale (frail: ≥3). The primary outcome was a composite poor 28-day outcome, defined by day-28 status as being in the intensive care unit, ongoing general-ward hospitalization, or death within 28 days. Separate multivariable logistic regression models using the same covariates and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were used to compare the two instruments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Among 151 older adults, 102 (67.5%) were classified as frail by the FRAIL Scale and 87 (57.6%) by the CFS. Poor 28-day outcome occurred in 18 patients (11.9%). It was more frequent among CFS-defined frail than non-frail patients (18.4% vs. 3.1%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.004), whereas the difference by FRAIL classification was not statistically significant (15.7% vs. 4.1%,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.058). After adjustment for age, sex, and polypharmacy, CFS-defined frailty was associated with higher odds of poor 28-day outcome (adjusted OR 5.99, 95% CI 1.26–28.42;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.024), whereas FRAIL-defined frailty was not significantly associated with the outcome (adjusted OR 3.63, 95% CI 0.76–17.41;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.107). The CFS showed an AUC of 0.823 (95% CI 0.702–0.944), compared with 0.696 (95% CI 0.579–0.813) for the FRAIL Scale; the difference between the AUCs was statistically significant (DeLong
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.034).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cohort, CFS ratings obtained during acute hospitalization showed higher discrimination for poor 28-day outcome than the FRAIL Scale and remained associated with the outcome after adjustment for age, sex, and polypharmacy. Given the limited number of events and assessment during acute illness rather than for pre-illness status, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, may not apply directly to standard pre-illness CFS assessment, and require validation in larger cohorts.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls are a leading cause of injury and loss of independence among older adults. Although exercise-based interventions can reduce fall risk, sustaining adherence is challenging. The adapted Lifestyle-integrated Functional Exercise (aLiFE) programme addresses this by embedding balance, strength and physical activity tasks into daily routines. However, acceptability depends on whether older adults perceive aLiFE as understandable, manageable, safe and relevant. This may be particularly important for older Chinese adults living in UK, whose language preferences, cultural beliefs, social contexts and health-related experiences may shape perceptions of falls prevention. This study explored initial acceptability and perceived feasibility of aLiFE among older Chinese adults and healthcare professionals in UK.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Community-dwelling older Chinese adults and healthcare partners were purposively recruited in Manchester, UK. Three focus groups with 18 older Chinese adults and three individual interviews with healthcare partners were conducted. Participants completed aLiFE Activity Acceptability Rating Scale and Short Falls Efficacy Scale-International. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and qualitative data were analysed inductively using Reflexive Thematic Analysis to identify patterns in participants’ views, concerns and recommendations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four main themes were identified: (1) Perceived feasibility and practicality of the lifestyle-integrated concept; (2) Usability and accessibility of programme delivery and materials; (3) Perceived burden and accessibility of programme documentation and (4) Acceptability and perceived capability of programme activities. The lifestyle-integrated approach was generally viewed positively as being flexible and compatible with daily routines. Some participants considered documentation burdensome and queried accessibility and credibility of written records. Visual materials and group-based, face-to-face teaching were preferred to written instructions alone. Some activities were viewed as less acceptable because of concerns about safety, confidence and physical discomfort, particularly where tasks involved more challenging balance or strength components. Differences were also observed between older participants and healthcare partners, the latter tending to take a more cautious view of challenging activities and potential risks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The aLiFE programme was generally perceived as feasible and acceptable among older Chinese adults and healthcare partners. Acceptability depended on how the concept, activities, materials and delivery format were understood and received. These findings provide insights to inform cultural adaptation of aLiFE for this population and support further refinement before wider implementation or evaluation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Assessing early-stage acceptability of the adapted version of the lifestyle-integrated functional exercise (aLiFE) programme among community-dwelling Chinese older adults in the UK

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Empty-nest status describes household circumstances and is used to identify older adults for administrative attention. We examined how its operationalisation affects classification coverage and the information it provides about concurrent depressive symptoms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) 2018 analysis included rural adults aged ≥60 years with living children and observed 10-item Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D-10) scores. Proximity-defined empty-nest status required no child living with or nearby the participant; co-residence-defined status required no co-resident child. We compared person-level, household-expanded, and Harmonized CHARLS constructions. Primary association analyses used multiple imputation with community-clustered inference (N = 5,847), with continuous CES-D-10 as the primary outcome and CES-D-10 ≥ 10 as the binary outcome. We assessed fixed-label classification and incremental information beyond a demographic and health benchmark. Complete-case associations were sensitivity analyses; household-composition and 2020 analyses were exploratory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 5,917 eligible participants, proximity status was classifiable for 41.5%, 67.5%, and 98.8% using person-level, household-expanded, and Harmonized constructions, respectively. The primary adjusted mean difference was 0.198 CES-D-10 points (95% confidence interval (CI) − 0.153 to 0.549); the binary-outcome odds ratio was 1.019 (0.897 to 1.158). Direct-label areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) were 0.493 for proximity and 0.495 for co-residence. Adding either label changed apparent AUC by less than 0.001; community-fold cross-validation similarly showed little incremental discrimination. In exploratory analyses, empty-nest participants living alone had higher scores than non-empty-nest participants (mean difference 1.208; 95% CI 0.429 to 1.987), but their direct comparison with empty-nest participants living with other non-spouse members was uncertain (0.858; −0.505 to 2.222).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among rural older adults with living children in this sample, classification coverage depended on how the empty-nest label was constructed, and the aggregate label conveyed little concurrent symptom information. Studies should report the label definition, construction route, and classification coverage; household status should not substitute for direct symptom information. Exploratory household-group differences warrant longitudinal study; these findings do not validate a screening or referral pathway.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Empty-nest operationalisation and depressive symptoms among rural older Chinese adults: a CHARLS study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PCC is widely recognised as an important approach to supporting QoL in nursing homes. However, staff’s ability to provide PCC may be influenced by leadership and working conditions. There is still limited knowledge of how staff themselves experience performing PCC to support residents’ QoL in everyday nursing home care. The aim of this study was to explore staff experiences of providing PCC to support resident QoL and how their provision of PCC is influenced by leadership and staff working conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative study design was used. Fifteen semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 enrolled nurses and five nursing assistants working in nursing homes in four Swedish municipalities between February and May 2024. Data were analysed using qualitative conventional content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      An overarching theme,
                      <jats:italic>Creating everyday meaning despite challenges</jats:italic>
                      , was supported by three categories:
                      <jats:italic>Building human relationships in care</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>Connecting through communication and teamwork</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic>Overcoming obstacles for person-centred care</jats:italic>
                      . Meaningful relationships, attentiveness and tailored support were described as central to providing PCC and supporting residents’ QoL. Communication and teamwork enabled staff to understand and respond to residents’ individual needs, while leadership contributed by supporting staff and facilitating teamwork. Organisational barriers, including staffing shortages, time pressure, communication difficulties and limited leadership support, constrained staff members’ ability to consistently provide PCC and support residents’ QoL.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Staff described a strong intrinsic commitment to providing PCC that supports residents’ QoL. However, their ability to do so was shaped by leadership and organisational conditions. Enabling PCC in nursing homes therefore requires not only staff commitment, but also supportive leadership, adequate staffing and work environments that allow time, communication and continuity in care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rural elderly individuals are a high-risk population for pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB). Medication adherence is critical for treatment success but is often compromised by low health literacy and high stigma. This study aimed to investigate whether stigma moderates the relationship between health literacy and medication adherence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In December 2024, a consecutive sampling method was used to recruit 283 rural elderly PTB patients who had completed four months of anti-tuberculosis treatment from 18 tuberculosis prevention and control institutions in Henan Province. Sociodemographic and clinical data were collected, and validated Chinese scales for health literacy, stigma, and medication adherence were used. Spearman correlation, simple linear regression, and hierarchical regression (controlling for 9 covariates) were performed to analyze main effects and moderating effects, followed by Johnson‑Neyman analysis and sensitivity analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Health literacy was positively correlated with medication adherence (ρ = 0.227,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), and stigma was negatively correlated with medication adherence (ρ = -0.210,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Hierarchical regression showed that the health literacy×stigma interaction term was significant (b = 0.005, 95% CI 0.001–0.008,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.010), whereas ordinal logistic regression yielded only marginal significance (OR = 1.004,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.061). Simple slope analysis indicated that the effect of health literacy was not significant at low stigma (b = 0.017,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.303) but was significant and stronger at high stigma (b = 0.076,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). The Johnson‑Neyman threshold was a raw stigma score > 2.72, exceeding which 63.25% of patients fell. Sensitivity analyses showed generally consistent patterns, although the ordinal logistic regression yielded only marginal significance, the moderation finding should therefore be considered exploratory.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The present study offers exploratory evidence suggesting that stigma may play a moderating role in the relationship between health literacy and medication adherence. This moderating pattern suggests that the association between health literacy and adherence may be more pronounced among rural elderly PTB patients with high stigma. Routine assessment of stigma and targeted health education for those with high stigma could be considered, although the efficacy of such stratified strategies remains to be validated by future interventional research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:p>Active community mobility is critical for preserving physical health, autonomy, and functional capacity in older adults. Participants wore a GPS device for seven consecutive days to objectively record all trips and travel modes. Data were integrated with household interview results and neighborhood-level census data (walkability and income).</jats:p>

Active travel significantly differed by education level and nutritional status (

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are among the principal observable expressions of psychological distress and unmet need in nursing home residents who can no longer reliably verbalize internal experiences, and recognizing their day-to-day variation underpins timely, person-centered care. Yet BPSD fluctuate across days, shifts, and contexts, while established instruments such as the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Nursing Home version (NPI-NH) assess them retrospectively over the preceding weeks or months. This mismatch leaves basic descriptive questions about the day-to-day symptom landscape in routine care unanswered. This study describes the prevalence, severity, co-occurrence, between-unit variation, and shift and weekday patterns of BPSD documented through structured daily registrations in nursing home care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Descriptive longitudinal observational study of 230 individuals with dementia in six nursing homes across six Swedish municipalities, followed for a median observation period of 270 days (interquartile range 120 to 446). Care staff used a digital tool to rate the severity (0–3) of twelve common BPSD, adapted from the NPI-NH, at the end of every work shift, yielding over one million symptom registrations. Analyses were descriptive and person-weighted, giving each individual equal weight regardless of observation length.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cumulative symptom prevalence (at any point during observation) ranged from 90% (agitation) to 70% (euphoria). Each symptom’s mean daily prevalence was much lower (4–18%), and symptoms were predominantly of low severity. At least one symptom was recorded on a median of 43.5% of registered days, varying widely between individuals. Clinically related symptoms tended to occur together, consistent with established NPI-NH domain structures, and the mean number of symptoms per day varied more than twofold across the six units. Symptoms were most frequent on evening shifts and least frequent at night, except sleep disturbances, with little variation across weekdays. Just under half of all possible shift registrations were completed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Daily registrations describe an intermittent and heterogeneous symptom landscape at a resolution that periodic assessments are not designed to provide. These findings provide an empirical baseline for future multilevel analyses and support BPSD monitoring that covers both individual symptoms and the daily number of symptoms in nursing homes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Available literature related to the association between orthostatic blood pressure (BP) variations and falls is controversial. We analyzed how orthostatic hypo- (OH) and hypertension (OHTN) relate to falls considering recovery time (RT) in community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This analysis uses data from the ActiFE cohort. BP was measured lying, immediately, 1, 2 and 3 min after standing. Systolic OH (sOH) and systolic OHTN (sOHTN) indicate a systolic BP (SBP) drop or increment ≥20 mm Hg, respectively. OH and OHTN further consider a diastolic BP (DBP) drop or increment ≥10 mm Hg. RT was categorized as Early Recovery ( < 1 min), Delayed Recovery (1-3 min), or No Recovery. Falls over 12 months were collected prospectively. Logistic regression examined associations with falls, adjusting for age, sex, diabetes, hemoglobin, instrumental activities of daily living, hand strength, fall risk-increasing drugs, past falls, Falls Efficacy Scale-International and anxiety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 509 subjects (mean age 79 years, 44% female, 168 falls), prevalences were: 16.5% sOH, 26.9% OH, 9.0% sOHTN and 15.5% OHTN. Overall, OH was not associated with falls. However, falls risk increased with Delayed (OR 3.11 [95% CI 1.21-8.01]) and NoRecovery (OR 4.04 [95% CI 1.07-15.26]). sOH showed an adjusted OR of 2.00 [95% CI 1.15-3.47] for at least one fall. Regarding RT the risk of falls was increased in Delayed (OR 4.73 [95% CI 1.71-13.10]) and No Recovery (OR 5.06 [95% CI 1.42-22.27]). OHTN was not associated with falls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, only sOH was associated with falls. When RT was considered, those with Delayed and No Recovery showed higher risk of falls regardless of the OH definition used.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Orthostatic blood pressure fluctuations and risk of falls in community-dwelling older adults: the role of recovery time

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The demographic shift toward an ageing population has increased focus on frailty. Frailty has become increasingly recognized as a critical factor in clinical decision-making and the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) has gained widespread use across healthcare settings. This study explores paramedics’ experiences using CFS for older patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study uses a qualitative research design and incorporates semi-structured interviews to explore paramedics’ experience of the feasibility and practical application of CFS in prehospital care. The study is part of a larger project on the use of CFS for older patients (≥ 65 years) in prehospital care in the North Denmark Region. During the study period 432 of 2 084 patients (21%) had a documented CFS score. CFS scores spanned all nine categories of the scale. The study is inspired from hermeneutic philosophy and frailty assessment theory. Individual face-to-face semi-structured interviews were conducted, and data was analysed using thematic analysis, inspired by Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of eleven paramedics participated in the interviews (ten men and one woman). The median age was 38 years, and participants had a median of 11 years of experience in the prehospital setting. Three main themes emerged: (1) Older patients – complexity and clinical assessment (2) Making CFS work in the prehospital practice (3) CFS as a shared language in cross-sector collaboration. Older patients were perceived as a complex and habitually ill population requiring an adapted clinical mindset. Distinction between acute illness and frailty was described as challenging in the prehospital setting. CFS was considered to serve as a bridge between sectors and professional discipline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CFS was generally perceived as relevant and as a tool that can support continuity of care and create a shared language around frailty. The findings highlight the importance of paramedics understanding the purpose and application of CFS and how the assessment may contribute to patient care across sectors. These considerations may be relevant when supporting the use of CFS in routine prehospital practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction: Sarcopenia, an age-related syndrome characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass, decreased muscle strength, and/or reduced physical performance, is associated with disruptions in amino acid and lipid metabolism. This study aimed to investigate serum metabolic alterations associated with sarcopenia in older adults. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 50 patients with sarcopenia (diagnosed per 2014 AWGS criteria) were matched 1:1 by age and sex with non-sarcopenic controls from a pool of 2,965 individuals. Assessments included skeletal muscle mass, grip strength, and gait speed. Serum metabolomic profiling was conducted using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). The screening of differential metabolites: variable importance in the projection (VIP) > 1 derived from the OPLS-DA model, and adjusted p-value based on false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 calculated by two-sample t-test. Results: Among 100 participants aged 60–87 years, individuals with sarcopenia showed significantly lower BMI, grip strength, albumin, and ASMI than controls (all p < 0.05), whereas lipid levels were comparable. PCA suggested weak group separation, whereas PLS-DA achieved clearer discrimination by sex and sarcopenia status. Differential metabolites identified in the sarcopenia group included arginine, leucine and histidinyl-histidine, the latter of which exhibited decreased abundance. Concomitant alterations in the levels of lipid metabolites collectively suggest disrupted amino acid and lipid metabolism. Conclusion: Patterns of dysregulated amino acid and fatty acid metabolism were observed in older adults with sarcopenia. Such metabolic disturbances might serve as candidate biomarkers to inform early detection and nutritional intervention strategies.</jats:p>
title: Serum Metabolomic Profiling Reveals Disrupted Amino Acid and Fatty Acid Metabolism in Older Adults with Sarcopenia

records.abstract: <jats:p>Background The heterogeneity within the group of older women challenges balancing overtreatment and undertreatment. The tumor-stroma ratio (TSR) has emerged as a potential prognostic marker. In this study, the prognostic value of the TSR in older women with breast cancer is investigated. Methods Women aged ≥70 years, diagnosed between 2003-2009 with hormone receptor-positive (HR+), human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2)-negative breast cancer were included, excluding those treated with chemotherapy or neoadjuvant therapy. Results Altogether, 2,974 women were included: 70% had a stroma-low tumor and 30% stroma-high. The likelihood of having a stroma-high tumor increased with age (p = 0.021). Univariable analyses presented worse overall survival (OS; HR 1.106, 95% CI 1.016-1.204, p = 0.020) and unfavorable metastasis-free period (MFP; HR 1.324, 95% CI 1.044-1.680, p = 0.021) in stroma-high patients, but this was not significant in multivariable analyses (OS: p = 0.080, MFP: p = 0.961). In multivariable analyses, the TSR remained prognostic regarding OS in women without relevant comorbidities (HR 1.376, 95% CI 1.144-1.655, p < 0.001), and with a ductal carcinoma and no adjuvant systemic therapy (HR 1.455, 95% CI 1.114-1.900, p = 0.006). Conclusion High stromal content was associated with worse OS and MFP and was especially an independent, unfavorable prognostic factor in patients without relevant comorbidities, and those with a ductal carcinoma and no adjuvant therapy. In these specific patient groups, the TSR could support further personalization of treatment, such as de-escalating therapy in those with favorable prognosis (stroma-low) or by treating those with an unfavorable prognosis (stroma-high) more aggressively.</jats:p>
title: The Prognostic Value of the Tumor-Stroma Ratio (TSR) is Most Pronounced in Older Breast Cancer Patients without Relevant Comorbidities

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Home-based reablement programs have improved everyday functioning for people living with early-stage dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but the substantial time commitment required for delivery by health professionals has created a barrier to widespread implementation. Digital technology could facilitate delivery, but traditional devices such as smartphones and tablets present usability challenges for this population. We have co-designed a cognitive reablement program, VOICE-COG, that can deliver personalized interventions broadcast via voice-controlled digital voice assistants (DVAs).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot nonblinded randomized controlled trial examined the feasibility and potential effectiveness of VOICE-COG for older adults living with dementia or MCI to guide the design of a full-scale trial.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults (aged 60‐85 years) with a self-reported diagnosis of dementia or MCI (N=30) were recruited via Facebook or the StepUp-for Dementia Research database and randomized to either a DVA intervention (n=15) or control (n=15) group for 12 weeks. Each participant randomized to the intervention group and their care partner met with a psychologist via Zoom to select 2 or 3 personalized goals from the VOICE-COG program. The personalized program was input into the software (BuddyLink) by researchers for broadcast via a DVA (Amazon Alexa Show 8). Participants in the control group received enhanced usual care, consisting of treatment as usual, plus weekly informational emails. Primary feasibility outcomes were recruitment, retention, device-recorded adherence, and the System Usability Scale (SUS). Secondary outcomes were self-reported by the participant and care partner via web-based Qualtrics forms and included the Goal Attainment Scale–Light (GAS), changes in participant mood, cognition, and everyday functioning, and carer burden.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The recruitment rate was 86% (30/35) and the retention rate was 97% (29/30), with 1 participant in the intervention group lost to follow-up. Adherence to the VOICE-COG program ranged from 29% to 100% (mean 70%, SD 17%). The VOICE-COG program was rated as marginally acceptable (mean SUS score 56.3, SD 18.1). After 12 weeks, 60% (9/15) of the intervention group reported having met or exceeded their goals (GAS-Light t-score ≥50; mean 57.6, SD 15.4). The intervention group had a significantly higher increase in Multifactorial Memory Questionnaire–Strategy subscale score compared with control, mean difference 5.0 (95% CI 0.03-10.1,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.049), representing a medium effect size (
                      <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>
                      =0.55). There were no other significant differences between groups.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This co-designed VOICE-COG program, delivered via DVAs, was feasible for older adults living with early-stage dementia or MCI, resulting in most participants meeting their reablement goals and increases in the use of memory strategies. System usability issues should be addressed in future adequately powered trials.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Feasibility of a Co-Designed Personalized Cognitive Reablement Program Delivered via Digital Voice Assistants for Older Adults Living With Early-Stage Dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) but did not significantly affect fear of personal failure (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.12) or human-machine ambiguity (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Fear-Specific Technophobia as a Mediator Between Daily Technical Support and Instrumental Versus Hedonic Technology Use in Later Life: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
