<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults often face challenges using digital transportation planning tools to engage in meaningful activities. In Sherbrooke, a Canadian city located in the province of Québec, hilly terrain, bus-based mobility, and varied digital literacy among older adults highlight the need for accessible transportation planning technologies. Despite the growing demand for accessible and inclusive technologies, interfaces are often not tailored to the specific needs and preferences of older adults, making them difficult to use. Addressing this gap is essential to support the mobility and social participation of older adults in their communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to enhance older adults’ experience with a transportation planning e-tool—called Mobilainés—by co-designing its interface and evaluating its usability and user experience in line with their needs and preferences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a participatory design approach, the study encompassed both development and evaluation phases, integrating qualitative and quantitative methods. In the development phase, heuristic evaluation, along with the Mobilaînés mock-up, was performed to identify the percentage of compatibility with age-friendly usability design principles and guidelines. Fourteen co-design workshops with the steering committee and research team informed persona development and core functionalities, while 3 workshops with older adults refined the mock-ups. For the evaluation phase, 2 laboratory usability tests (simulated context) and 1 in-field test (real-world context) were conducted with 5, 7, and 4 older adults, respectively. Data were collected using a combination of objective performance metrics recorded in real time by a computer and subjective user feedback, gathered using the System Usability Scale, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology questionnaires, and focus group discussions. For the in-field testing, user experience data were obtained via the User Experience Questionnaire and semistructured interviews. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative data were analyzed thematically.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The participatory design and iterative evaluation process identified key design decisions for age-friendly transportation planning, including step-by-step navigation, simplified task flow, clear feedback, visual clarity, and personalization. In the final laboratory usability test, the Mobilaînés e-tool showed 84% compatibility with age-friendly guidelines, a 97% task completion rate, and System Usability Scale and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology scores corresponding to very good usability. In-field User Experience Questionnaire results and interviews suggested that participants perceived the e-tool as reliable, easy to use, and accurate, despite the lack of real-time data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participatory design and iterative usability testing revealed that older adults’ experience with Mobilainés transportation planning e-tools is improved. These design learnings contributed to improved usability and confidence in real-world travel planning, offering practical guidance for the development of age-friendly digital transportation tools. Future research should explore collaborative and technological strategies to support its adoption and sustained use, particularly among older adults with limited digital literacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Development and Evaluation of a Transportation Planning e-Tool for Older Adults: Co-Design Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging is a global phenomenon that has led to a rise in age-related conditions, particularly dementia. This situation presents significant challenges for health care systems, caregivers, and society as a whole. Technologies have shown potential to address the needs of people living with dementia and their caregivers, offering support in daily activities, communication, and care monitoring. However, only a quarter of countries worldwide have developed national dementia plans, and even fewer have integrated technology-based solutions into these policies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to analyze existing gaps in dementia plans, with a particular emphasis on the limited integration of technological solutions as essential tools for dementia care and management. Based on this analysis, this study proposes a framework to facilitate context-appropriate technology integration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study presents a narrative review of public policy frameworks for dementia care. The review provides a global overview, examines the context in Latin America, and focuses on Mexico as a case study to analyze how technology is integrated into dementia strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Based on these findings, this study proposes a framework of general recommendations adaptable across multiple countries. Furthermore, it demonstrates the application of this framework in Mexico to strengthen its national dementia strategy through technological solutions tailored to people living with dementia and their informal caregivers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Given that dementia is recognized as a global priority, countries with aging populations have developed numerous technological solutions. These international experiences serve as valuable references to guide the adoption or rejection of specific approaches, provided that local cultural and social contexts are considered. The applied technologies were merged into a framework that can be adapted to different countries, taking into account social aspects, governance, and region-specific barriers to generate a viable, customized option, as demonstrated in the case study focused on Mexico.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Global Frameworks Toward Effective Integration of Technology in National Dementia Strategies: Narrative Review and Case Study in Mexico

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While telecare has considerable potential to improve home care services, benefit older adults, and support informal caregivers, its adoption remains limited. There is also a notable gap in empirical research on the factors that influence informal caregivers’ behavioral intention to use telecare. In particular, existing theoretical acceptance models are insufficiently comprehensive, as they do not specifically address informal caregivers of older adults and have largely overlooked the psychosocial outcomes of engaging with telecare.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the behavioral intention of Slovenian informal caregivers of older adults to use telecare, focusing on the preuse stage of technology acceptance, by integrating the perceived psychosocial outcomes of telecare engagement (peace of mind, reduced anxiety, sense of safety, and perceived connectedness with the care recipient) into the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study applied nested ordinary least squares regression analysis to survey data collected in 2021 in Slovenia from informal caregivers of older adults, all of whom were aged 40 years or older. Of 612 respondents in the dataset, 558 were retained after excluding current or former users of care-related assistive technologies; the regression analyses were based on the 526 participants with complete data on all model variables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The regression analysis used 3 nested models to examine predictors of the intention of informal caregivers of older adults to use telecare. The first model, which included only background variables (burden of care, financial coping, and caregiver sociodemographic characteristics), had limited explanatory power (
                      <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                      ²=0.03), with financial coping as the only significant predictor (β=−0.14,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.005). Adding UTAUT predictors significantly improved the model’s fit (
                      <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                      ²=0.49). Performance expectancy (β=0.52,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), facilitating conditions (β=0.11,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.005), and social influence (β=0.21,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) emerged as additional significant predictors. Incorporating perceived psychosocial outcomes further improved the model’s fit and increased the explained variance (
                      <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                      ²=0.54); this additional factor also showed the strongest association (β=0.41,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). Patterns for the other predictors remained consistent across models, but including perceived psychosocial outcomes substantially reduced the coefficient for performance expectancy.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional sample, perceived psychosocial outcomes were the predictors most strongly associated with behavioral intention in the extended UTAUT model, indicating that they may be important factors in understanding telecare acceptability among informal caregivers. The findings suggest that developers, policymakers, and health and social care providers should consider not only functional aspects of telecare but also the psychosocial needs of informal caregivers. As the study measured self-reported intention at the preuse stage rather than actual use, longitudinal and behavioral research is needed to establish whether these associations translate into telecare adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Integrating Perceived Psychosocial Outcomes Into the Assessment of Telecare Acceptability Among Slovenian Informal Caregivers of Older People: Cross-Sectional Survey Study

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior research has examined the relationship between traumatic experiences and cognitive function in adulthood. We build on this literature by using a life course perspective to ask whether incident multimorbidity mediates the relationship between lifetime trauma and trajectories of cognitive function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We use latent growth curve models and data from the 2010-2020 waves of the Health and Retirement Study (N = 16,662) to examine the relationship between lifetime trauma, incident multimorbidity, and the intercept and slope of cognitive function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results indicate that trauma is associated with a higher intercept of cognitive function and greater cognitive decline. Lifetime trauma is also associated with higher risk of incident multimorbidity, which, in turn, is associated with a lower intercept of cognitive function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Incident multimorbidity has an upstream influence on poor cognitive function among people exposed to trauma. Interventions may be needed for people exposed to trauma over the life course to reduce the risk of disease and cognitive decline in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Caregiving for older adults imposes substantial physical and emotional costs, yet less attention has been paid to how disruptions in personally valued activities and caregiver–care recipient relationship quality relate to caregivers’ psychological well-being over time. Drawing on the activity restriction model and conservation of resource theory, this longitudinal study examined how within-person changes in disrupted valued activities (DVA) and negative relationship quality (NRQ) influence caregivers’ resilience and positive affect.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data came from three waves of the National Study of Caregiving, linked to the National Health and Aging Trends Study. The analytic sample included 2,415 caregivers who provided 3,441 caregiver-wave observations, nested within 1,559 care recipients. Three-level linear mixed models decomposed DVA and NRQ into between-person and within-person components and adjusted for caregiver characteristics, care-recipient dementia status, and activities of daily living (ADL) limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Resilience and positive affect showed substantial variation between-person and within-person. Higher average and higher-than-usual DVA were each associated with lower positive affect and resilience. Higher average NRQ was associated with lower positive affect and resilience, whereas higher-than-usual NRQ was associated with lower positive affect but not resilience. Care-recipient dementia status and ADL limitations were not associated with either outcome once caregiver characteristics were considered.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DVA and NRQ appear to be distinct sources of resource loss, independently linked to lower caregiver well-being across and within caregivers over time. Interventions may be effective by targeting either the maintenance of meaningful activities or improvements in relationship quality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Disrupted Activities and Caregivers' Resilience and Positive Affect

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Qualitative research is central to understanding aging-related experiences, yet expectations for rigor are often unclear and inconsistently applied across studies. Here, we introduce the Rigor in Qualitative Research Framework, developed through a structured review of qualitative quality frameworks and reporting guidance and application to qualitative articles published in Innovation in Aging. We identified ten domains of qualitative rigor that reflect core areas across qualitative approaches: methodological coherence, relevance and contribution, contextual sensitivity and transferability, researcher reflexivity and positioning, participant/data-item selection and composition, ethical and relational integrity, data generation quality and richness, analytic rigor and transparency, interpretive credibility and evidence linkage, and reporting clarity, coherence, and usability. We then examined how these domains are described and operationalized in 39 published qualitative studies from 2020-2025 in Innovation in Aging, identifying exemplars in how rigor is enacted in practice. Findings suggest that existing frameworks provide broad coverage of key domains but differ in scope, emphasis, and level of guidance; qualitative studies thus vary in how clearly and consistently these domains are articulated. In response, our proposed framework integrates these domains into a structure supporting both evaluation and application, while remaining flexible to different epistemological and methodological traditions. The Rigor in Qualitative Research Framework is intended to guide study design, analysis, and reporting, and to support more consistent evaluation during peer review, providing a practical reference point for qualitative research across applied health and gerontology.</jats:p>
title: The rigor in qualitative research framework: A practical guide to evaluating qualitative studies

                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Young adults are the caregivers of tomorrow. However, it remains unclear what stereotypes about informal caregiving for older adults they have learned.                   <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants aged 18 to 35 years, collected from the community (sample 1) and university students (sample 2) in Canada answered a self-reported online survey on public caregiver stigma (Public Caregiver Stigma Scale, Warmth-Competence-Scale) and their sociodemographic background.                   <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>: The EFA performed on sample 1 resulted in a two-factor model with correlated factors that was confirmed by a CFA in sample 2, demonstrating excellent model fit. Content and concurrent validity were supported by the study’s findings and internal consistency of the two scales varied between acceptable and good. Young adults showed moderately high positive and negative public caregiver stigma, which were associated with their sociodemographic characteristics.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study confirmed a new quantitative measure of public caregiver stigma targeting unpaid caregiving for older adults, reflecting negative (e.g., isolation, invisibility) and positive (e.g., admiration) stereotypes, emotional, and behavioral reactions.                   <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The aim of this study was to evaluate whether a balance-focused multimodal exercise programme improves balance and reduces falls for people with mild cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A single-blind randomised controlled trial (n = 128, before withdrawals), with 6-month intervention, followed by 6-month maintenance period. The intervention, Balance on the Brain, consisted of three exercise programmes: walking, Balance Yourself and Clock Yourself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data from 126 adults with mild cognitive impairment were included in the study (median age = 76, 63% female). The study did not meet the required sample size to be fully powered for either falls or balance primary outcomes. Therefore, the lack of significant between-group differences for the primary outcomes of falls or balance at 6 and 12-months remains inconclusive, due to insufficient power. Fifty-nine percent (n = 38) of intervention participants were identified as adherers. Adherers’ balance improved significantly compared to low-adherers/controls at 6 and 12-months and intervention adherers fell less than low-adherers/controls, although the difference was not significant. However, the adherers data were exploratory and need to be used with caution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Balance on the Brain was underpowered and as such the non-significant primary balance and falls outcomes should be interpreted as inconclusive for people living with mild cognitive impairment in the community. Those who adhered demonstrated improved balance, and reduced falls compared to low-adherers/controls, however these data should be interpreted as exploratory and with caution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates how health status shapes the age trajectories of informal caregiving for spouses and older parents in England.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The data came from five waves (2012–2023) of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). We analysed 41,997 person-wave observations from 12,420 individuals aged 50+. We derived a latent health construct via hierarchical confirmatory factor analysis, integrating functional, mental, physical, and cognitive domains. Dynamic random-effects models were employed to examine the influence of prior health on consequent caregiving, and initial condition adjustment was made to correct estimation bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among those with a spouse, parents, or parents-in-law, healthier individuals demonstrated steeper increases in caregiving probability over time, while those in poor health showed flatter or declining caregiving trajectories. For spousal caregiving, better health was associated with a lower likelihood of caregiving at age 50, but this relationship turned positive from age 70 onwards. For parental caregiving, better health was associated with a higher likelihood of caregiving from age 53 onwards.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall the research findings are consistent with the healthy caregiver hypothesis, particularly in later life. Good health facilitates the provision of informal care, whereas poor health compromises caregiving capability and constitutes a barrier to taking on a caregiving role. A healthier older population not only means lower care needs but also has greater capacity to provide care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Age trajectories of informal caregiving for older people in England: Testing the healthy caregiver hypothesis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Increasing attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) have left many researchers and educators in aging scrambling on how best to navigate this political landscape in their research and teaching. In response, the Gerontological Society of America (GSA)’s Public Policy Advisory Panel convened a multidisciplinary panel discussion of experts from the six GSA member groups and three advisory panels in November 2025 to discuss the current state of the research and education, particularly as it relates to diversity in health and aging; current efforts by researchers and educators to adapt and respond to these efforts; and future actionable recommendations on how to continue to support DEI principles in all phases of health and aging research and education. Several common themes emerged across disciplines (collaboration, education, mentorship, and research) that led to four key recommendations: (1) cultivate authentic community relationships and collaboration; (2) intentionally engage historically excluded populations; (3) innovate; and (4) invoke national and state professional and competency standards. Ultimately, this multidisciplinary convening and its ensuing recommendations provide gerontological researchers and educators with both context and guidance for navigating recent attacks on DEI and contribute to a broader conversation on this important topic.</jats:p>
title: Supporting Diversity in Health and Aging Research and Education: Recommendations from a Multidisciplinary Gerontological Symposium

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rise of transnational families has generated new care arrangements in which migrant children use digital technologies to support ageing parents across borders. While the functional role of digital technologies in facilitating remote care is well documented, their relational and culturally embedded dimensions remain less understood. This review synthesises recent evidence on how digital technologies shape transnational caregiving.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eight electronic sources were systematically searched for studies on transnational families, ageing, digital technology (including artificial intelligence—AI), and care, published between 2020 and 2025. Eligible studies were extracted, coded, and analysed using thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the analysis. Five themes were identified: 1) adoption and challenges for transnational ICT-mediated care; 2) ambivalence towards digital intimacy; 3) emotional labour and strategic concealment in transnational family care; 4) cultural norms and moral hierarchies of digital care; 5) structural inequalities in transnational care. Digital technologies both foster connection and amplify separation, serving as symbolic markers of family devotion and tools for managing information across generations. Rather than democratising care, technologies often reinforce existing global North–South, gendered, and class-based inequalities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Digital technologies both sustain and transform transnational care, yet digitally mediated care remains relational and structurally constrained. Stronger digital inclusion and coordinated cross-border care infrastructures are needed to support ageing transnational families, while avoiding the reproduction of existing social, gendered, and global inequalities, and enabling older adults to age with dignity, connection, and security.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Caring across borders: ageing and digital technology in transnational families

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Caregiver burden significantly impedes self-care, often resulting in poor health and increased vulnerability to chronic illness. Despite these risks, the underlying factors influencing caregivers’ self-care remain understudied. This qualitative descriptive study explored the context of caregiver self-care and identified perceived barriers and facilitators to practicing self-care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted four focus groups with 14 caregivers primarily responsible for providing in-home care to older adults (≥ 65 years) with chronic illnesses. Focus groups were audio-recorded and transcribed. A hierarchical coding system was developed and refined using the focus group guide and preliminary transcript review. Coded transcripts were analyzed using an iterative inductive-deductive thematic approach based on established theories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Caregivers’ multi-dimensional definitions of self-care shaped their perceived barriers and facilitators. Three core determinants of self-care behaviors were identified: capability (caregivers’ psychological and physical health, and behavioral regulation); motivation (caregiver identity, emotions, and perceived control); and opportunity (social and environmental influences and resources). Caregivers recognized that self-care deficits negatively affect their clinical, behavioral, and psychosocial outcomes. These results informed the development of a conceptual framework for caregiver self-care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings underscore the importance of integrating caregivers’ own perceptions of self-care into support models. Interventions should transition toward personalized approaches that address both intrinsic psychological drivers and extrinsic environmental constraints. The framework derived from this study provides a theory-driven roadmap that informs future interventions, ensuring support systems align with caregivers’ unique needs and contexts to foster better self-care and ultimately enhance their health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Determinants of Self-Care Practices Among Family Caregivers of Older Adults with Chronic Illness: A Qualitative Descriptive Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the IHSS+ ADRD Training Project, a multilingual intervention for caregivers serving individuals living with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) through California’s In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) program, using the RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A quasi-experimental, mixed-methods evaluation was conducted from July 2019 to June 2024 across Alameda and Los Angeles counties. By applying the RE-AIM framework, Reach and Effectiveness dimensions were assessed through surveys completed by 488 caregivers in English (n = 297), Spanish (n = 102), and Chinese (n = 89) at pre-training, post-training, and 3-month follow-up. Caregivers were diverse among English speakers (38% Black/African American, 23% Hispanic/Latino, and 20% Asian), averaged 49.9 years old, and were predominantly women (88%). Quantitative measures assessed dementia knowledge, self-efficacy, distress, and depression. Qualitative interviews with stakeholders (n = 11) and open-ended caregiver survey responses explored Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance dimensions</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RE-AIM findings demonstrated: Reach across diverse caregiver populations in multilingual formats; Effectiveness with significant improvements in dementia knowledge and self-efficacy sustained at 3-month follow-up, plus 88-99% satisfaction; Adoption facilitated by union partnership; Implementation successfully transitioned to virtual delivery during COVID-19 despite technology barriers; and Maintenance supported by increased caregiver confidence, self-care awareness, and stress management skills, though sustainability required ongoing funding.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Language-concordant training produced meaningful, sustained improvements across a diverse paid caregiver workforce, demonstrating its value as an equity strategy in home care workforce development. While virtual delivery was feasible and cost-effective, long-term success depends on securing dedicated funding and reliable technology infrastructure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Interest in retirement planning among university faculty has grown in recent years as more academics approach traditional retirement age. This scoping review examines the current literature on retirement planning among higher education faculty by examining study characteristics; participant characteristics; theoretical frameworks employed; factors influencing retirement planning; and the quality of the included studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A comprehensive search across Medline, Embase, APA PsycInfo, AgeLine, ERIC, Education Source, Business Source Premier, Sociological Abstracts, International Bibliography of the Social Sciences, JSTOR, and Web of Science Core Collection yielded an initial dataset of 8,906 unique articles. Following full-text assessment, 44 studies met the inclusion criteria.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five factors prevailed across this literature as key mechanisms in academic retirement planning, including: 1) financial security; 2) health factors; 3) age and/or institutional policies; 4) work, family, and lifestyle factors; and 5) professional identity. Participant characteristics such as age, gender, stage of retirement, and other characteristics of the academic environment were reported inconsistently across the literature; only 14 of the studies mentioned a theoretical framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is the first scoping review of academic retirement with a focus on planning that includes a range of methods. While health and financial security remain central to retirement planning broadly, the studies in this review suggest that professional identity plays a distinct role in shaping how academics approach retirement planning. Implications include the need for longitudinal designs to capture how faculty transitions, shifting professional identities, and planning behaviors evolve dynamically over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Drafting the next chapter: A scoping review of academic retirement planning

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social isolation is an urgent public health concern, especially for older immigrants who face heightened barriers to social participation due to disability, structural health inequities, and limited access to culturally and linguistically appropriate services. This study presents a programmatic model that explains how social connection and sustained participation can be fostered through accessible, culturally responsive, and participatory design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This community-engaged case study examines a national virtual program serving Spanish-speaking older adults, many of whom have sensory disabilities and chronic illnesses. A thematic and comparative analysis was conducted using qualitative interviews with ten older adults with vision impairment, program documents, and consultation with program leadership. This led to the identification of a programmatic model, the emergent connections platform.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The emergent connections platform strengthens loosely connected social networks among older adults who share cultural and lived experiences through three pillars. The first is cultural, linguistic, and physically accessible infrastructure. Second, shared governance cultivates member leadership and program co-creation. Third, a flexible structure allows for evolution in response to member needs and innovations. These pillars collectively create pathways for individuals to engage, lead, and strengthen their communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advancing a more inclusive democracy requires sustained investment in accessible, community-led initiatives that support the leadership and innovation of marginalized older adults. This calls for moving towards models that position older adults as co-creators of programs and services. Doing so cultivates social connection through leadership, reciprocity, and a sense of belonging within a broader social fabric.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The extant literature suggests that spending time helping others is associated with both beneficial and detrimental effects on givers’ emotional experiences. To reconcile these findings, the current study examined the daily- and monthly-level associations between spending time helping others and well-being. We predicted that spending time helping others would be associated with lower hedonic well-being at the daily level but higher eudaimonic well-being at the monthly level. We further hypothesized that age would moderate these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used data from the main survey and the National Study of Daily Experiences (NSDE) in MIDUS 3 (N=865) and MIDUS Refresher 1 (N=612). Participants reported their daily and monthly time spent helping others. Measures included hedonic well-being (negative affect and positive affect) and eudaimonic well-being (social and psychological well-being).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At the daily level, our sample of adults experienced mixed emotional consequences on days when they spent more time helping others, reporting both higher negative and positive affect. Age moderation showed young and middle-aged adults experienced more negative affect. At the monthly level, spending time helping others was associated with higher social and psychological well-being. This association was significantly stronger among older adults than middle-aged adults in Refresher 1. Monthly spending time helping others was not associated with hedonic well-being.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that spending time helping others can be both taxing and enjoyable in the short term while contributing to eudaimonic benefits over the long term. Older age may reduce costs and enhance benefits of spending time helping others.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Spending time helping others and well-being of givers: Age differences in immediate and long-term effects on well-being

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior research finds that women spend more years than men caring for older relatives and friends (“lifetime family caregiving”) in the United States. This study examines whether these amounts have changed in recent years (2023 vs. 2011) and how recent estimates differ for men and women by relationship to the care recipient and type of care provided.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We update and expand previously published estimates, drawing upon the National Study of Caregiving (n=1,972 in 2011; n=6,500 in 2021-2023) and the Current Population Survey. We use a demographic technique to calculate years of remaining life men and women ages 20+ would provide family caregiving to an older adult if current age-specific rates held.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In 2023, lifetime family caregiving for an older adult was nearly three years longer for women relative to men: 7.1 (95%CI: 6.2,8.0) vs. 4.2 (95%CI: 3.7,4.7) (p&lt;.001). For women, estimates for lifetime family caregiving were a year higher in 2023 than in 2011 (p=.03); for men, estimates were nearly identical in both years. In 2023, lifetime family caregiving for an older spouse or partner was similar for women and men but was higher for women than for men for caring for a parent, grandparent, and other relationship and for personal, household, transportation, and medical tasks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:p>Older Australian adults commonly engage in formal and informal volunteering. We examine how volunteering relates to social support, a combined measure of an individual’s quantity of social interactions, and satisfaction with the quality of social relationships.</jats:p>

Idealization of youth and pervasive ageist and ableist narratives devalue aging, contributing to perceptions of later life and potentially fostering grief over lost opportunities. records.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to compare the differences in life-space activities among older Japanese drivers based on self-reported driving engagement in relatively difficult situations. This is a cross-sectional cohort study of 12,309 community-dwelling older drivers (mean [SD] age, 72.5 [5.1] years; 54.5% female). Driving engagement was assessed using yes/no questions regarding six driving situations, including rain, dark nights, and unfamiliar roads. Responses to the situations were categorized as “not driving,” “driving with anxiety,” and “driving without anxiety.” The Active Mobility Index (AMI) assessed the life-space and activities from respondents’ home. Analysis of covariance showed that driving with anxiety and not driving in some situations were significantly lower AMI scores compared to driving without anxiety (p < 0.05), especially in those who drive ≥ 4 situations.                     <jats:p>Intergenerational support plays a crucial role in mental health in later life, yet both the heterogeneity of support patterns and the symptom-level interplay among depressive symptoms remain underexplored.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>
                      Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS 2020,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                      = 7,444), Latent Class Analysis (LCA) identified intergenerational support patterns. Network analysis and the Network Comparison Test (NCT) were utilized to estimate and compare depressive symptom networks (CESD-10) across subgroups.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three patterns emerged: Distant-Supportive (55.9%), Proximate-Interactive (24.2%), and Traditional Co-resident (19.9%). While “sadness” and “being bothered” were universal core symptoms, NCT revealed distinct structural disparities. The Proximate-Interactive group exhibited a uniquely strong “bothered–fearful” connection. The Distant-Supportive group showed pronounced “effort–cannot get going” pathways, whereas the Traditional Co-resident group displayed a stronger “bothered–trouble focusing” link.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intergenerational support patterns are not only associated with overall depression severity but also with differences in the network topology of depressive symptoms. Differentiated interventions tailored to specific family structures are essential for geriatric mental health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

records.abstract: <jats:p>The aim of this study was to gain insight into young dementia carer-specific content provided on the websites of dementia and (young) carers organizations in seven European countries including: the UK, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Portugal, Ireland and Sweden. Research questions were: 1). What types of young dementia carer-specific content are available on national websites of dementia and (young) carers organizations across Europe? and 2). How does the content address the complex impact that dementia can have on young dementia carers? The identification of websites was informed by the contextual characteristics of each country in relation to dementia and young carers support and services. A standard protocol describing the website inclusion and exclusion criteria, data extraction and content analysis using a categorical coding framework was followed. Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarize data within and across countries. A total of 312 organizations with active websites meeting the eligibility criteria across countries were identified, and their websites reviewed. Content relevant to young dementia carers was identified in 28% (n = 86) of the websites, with uneven availability of resources across Europe and very limited resources in some countries. Most contents addressed five categories: Diagnosis & symptoms, Uncertainty & family distress, Changes in roles, Stigma & isolation and Identifying need for support. A lack of tailored resources to support young dementia carers was identified, particularly in relation to two categories: Grief & loss and Education & life planning. Only a minority of websites included young dementia carer-specific content. These websites primarily focused on general support needs and explanations of dementia, while key areas such as guidance on school, career, and life planning remain underdeveloped. There is a need for greater recognition of young dementia carers, clearer terminology, and more developmentally appropriate and practically oriented resources to strengthen online support for these carers across Europe.</jats:p>
title: Content Analysis of Free Online Information and Support Available to Young Dementia Carers Across Europe

                    <jats:p>Spirituality is a core component of person-centred dementia care, yet spiritual needs may be under-recognised as cognition and communication decline. Spiritual Reminiscence Therapy (SRT) is a structured intervention that emphasises meaning-making and existential reflection rather than autobiographical recall alone. We examined the clinical outcomes and implementation characteristics of SRT in older adults with dementia.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scoping review was conducted using Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. Electronic databases (Cochrane, EMBASE, MEDLINE, PubMed and PsycINFO) were searched from inception to 26 December 2025, supplemented by grey literature and reference screening. Eligible English-language quantitative and qualitative studies evaluating SRT in adults aged ≥65 years with dementia were included. Data were synthesised descriptively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four studies met inclusion criteria (2 qualitative, 1 randomized controlled trial, 1 prospective cohort study). SRT was associated with improvements in spiritual well-being, life meaning and hope. Psychological outcomes suggested increased life satisfaction and reduced depressive symptoms. Qualitative findings indicated enhanced social connectedness in residential care settings. Evidence for cognitive benefit was inconsistent and clinically modest, and functional outcomes were rarely assessed. Reporting of intervention delivery and implementation processes was variable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SRT may improve meaning-related and depressive symptoms in persons with dementia, however extant evidence is limited and methodologically heterogenous. Future research prioritizing standardised outcomes, longer follow-up and formal implementation evaluation are needed before broader integration into routine psychogeriatric practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:p>This study aimed to assess the recorded prevalence of a dementia diagnosis and the receipt of appropriate dementia care among current Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients of Aboriginal and Community Controlled Health Services (ACCHS) aged 45 and over, as documented in medical records. ACCHSs are Australian primary healthcare organisations that are initiated, governed and operated by local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. A manual audit of medical records was undertaken by a staff member from each participating ACCHS to identify current clients with a documented diagnosis of dementia and examine their receipt of key elements of dementia-related care. Across 9 ACCHSs located in New South Wales, a total of 70 clients with a recorded diagnosis of dementia were identified (1.2% recorded prevalence rate). The majority of clients with a dementia diagnosis had documented receipt of elements of appropriate dementia care including an active chronic disease management plan (61%), annual health assessment (56%), referral to aged care services (69%), and assessment of one or more dementia-related risks (94%). However, less than half of clients had a documented cognitive assessment within the last 12 months (41%) or completed any advance planning documentation (37%). Clients with a dementia diagnosis received a mean of 3.6 out of 6 assessed elements of best practice dementia care. As with primary care nationally and internationally, ACCHSs require co-designed support strategies to enhance their processes for dementia diagnosis and documentation and to build upon their delivery of best-practice dementia care. Priority dementia care areas for older clients with a confirmed dementia diagnosis include the evaluation of dementia-related risks such as elder abuse and driving safety, and the implementation of advance care planning including discussion or completion of relevant legal documents.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>Epigenetic aging algorithms are emerging tools for understanding the biological effects of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). A growing body of literature has applied DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks in people living with HIV (PWH) across the life course, examining epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) in relation to HIV infection, antiretroviral therapy (ART), comorbidities, and clinical biomarkers (e.g., viral load, CD4 T-cell counts). This systematic review (Prospero: CRD420251126874) summarizes and synthesizes the current evidence on epigenetic aging in PWH across the life course and identifies critical knowledge gaps for future research. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Medline through June 26, 2026. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and assessed studies for risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. We created a narrative synthesis of results and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA. Fifty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. More than half (n = 33) examined EAA in PWH compared to an uninfected control population. We identified heterogeneity in study populations and design, biospecimens profiled, platforms used for DNA methylation analysis, and epigenetic clocks employed. Only 6 studies included participants younger than 18 years and no studies focused exclusively on individuals over 65 years. Only 10 studies examined longitudinal changes in EAA. Thirty-seven papers evaluated associations between EAA and comorbidities. A meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA across 14 studies found a mean difference of 3.41 years (95%CI 2.22, 4.60) in PWH relative to controls. Current evidence supports accelerated EAA among PWH but highlights substantial methodological heterogeneity and important knowledge gaps. Longitudinal studies of EAA in PWH are needed in populations under 18 and over 65, to clarify the effects of ART, clinical biomarkers, and age-related comorbidities, and determine the clinical utility of epigenetic aging biomarkers.</jats:p>
title: Epigenetic aging in people with HIV across the life course: a systematic review and meta-analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Geriatric syndromes such as frailty may be more prevalent and occur earlier in people aging with HIV, negatively impacting outcomes like cognition. Cross-sectional data show strong associations between pre-frailty/frailty and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND). However, prospective studies suggest baseline HAND increases frailty risk, while pre-frailty/frailty do not predict HAND onset. We aimed to investigate longitudinal association between baseline frailty and HAND category progression. Longitudinal analysis of 194 participants aged ≥50 years from Mexico City referral center. Two standardized geriatric assessments performed at least one year apart. HAND defined using Antinori criteria, frailty by Fried phenotype. Inverse probability weighted Cox models adjusted for confounders from directed acyclic graph (age, educational level, detectable viral load, diabetes, stroke, ischemic heart disease) determined association between frailty and HAND progression. Median age 55 (53–61) years; 167 (86%) men; median follow-up 2.3 (1.6–3.1) years. Baseline: 129 (66.4%) robust, 62 (31.9%) pre-frail, 3 (1.5%) frail. No longitudinal association between pre-frailty/frailty and HAND progression was observed in this cohort (32 progression events; adjusted HR = 0.63, 95% CI 0.27–1.48; p = 0.29). No evidence of a prospective association between prefrailty/frailty and HAND category progression was observed in this cohort; most participants remained cognitively stable. To our knowledge, this is the first study describing HAND trajectories and their relationship with prefrailty/frailty in older adults with HIV in Mexico and Latin America.</jats:p>
title: Longitudinal Association Between Prefrailty/Frailty and HIV-associated Neurocognitive Disorder (HAND): a Mexican Prospective Study

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction: This study aimed to evaluate the dose–response relationship between the Oxidative Balance Score (OBS) and a novel Gompertz law-based biological age (GOLD BioAge) and to quantify the potential mediating contributions of the Systemic Inflammation Response Index (SIRI) and uric acid to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (UHR). Methods: This cross-sectional study included 20,930 adults aged ≥20 years (weighted mean age: 47.79 years) from seven cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2001–2010 and 2015–2018). Survey-weighted regressions were used to estimate independent associations of OBS with GOLD BioAge and Accelerated GOLD BioAge. Restricted cubic spline analysis was performed to assess potential nonlinearity. Robustness was assessed through sensitivity and stratified subgroup analyses. Exploratory mediation analyses using a bootstrap resampling-based framework were performed separately for SIRI and UHR to quantify their potential mediating contributions. Results: The weighted proportion of Accelerated GOLD BioAge in the overall sample was 37.57%. The OBS was inversely and linearly associated with GOLD BioAge (P for nonlinearity = 0.723). In the fully adjusted models, each 1-point increment in OBS was associated with a 0.11-year lower GOLD BioAge (β = −0.11, 95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.13 to −0.10, P < 0.001) and 5% lower odds of Accelerated GOLD BioAge (odds ratio [OR] = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.94 to 0.96, P < 0.001). Compared with the lowest OBS tertile (T1), the highest tertile (T3) had 51% lower odds of Accelerated GOLD BioAge (OR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.43 to 0.56, P for trend < 0.001). The inverse association was directionally consistent across examined subgroups, although its magnitude differed by sex (P for interaction < 0.001). Exploratory mediation analyses showed that SIRI and UHR accounted for 21.10% and 8.30% of the OBS–GOLD BioAge association, respectively. Conclusions: In a nationally representative sample, higher OBS was linearly associated with lower GOLD BioAge, with SIRI and UHR statistically accounting for part of this association. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that a comprehensive antioxidant-oriented dietary and lifestyle profile is associated with lower biological age, warranting further prospective investigation.</jats:p>
title: Association of the Oxidative Balance Score with GOLD BioAge: Potential Mediating Roles of SIRI and UHR among US Adults

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction. While residential greenspace has been linked to better cognitive function in older adults, it remains unclear whether short-term greenspace exposure during everyday mobility can provide immediate cognitive benefits. Stress may play a critical role in this process, as it reflects a mismatch between environmental demands and personal resources and may signal an increased need for restoration. Methods. This ambulatory assessment study examined the association between greenspace exposure and cognition in daily life, as well as the moderating role of stress. Over a two-week period, 123 older adults (aged 65–89 years) wore a GPS device that continuously recorded their mobility trajectories and carried a smartphone to complete repeated working memory tasks and experience sampling assessments of stressors approximately every two hours (seven times per day). Results. Multilevel models showed that, at the within-person level, greater-than-usual greenspace exposure in the past two hours was associated with higher-than-usual momentary working memory performance when stressor occurrence was reported, compared to moments when stressors were not reported. At the between-person level, individuals with higher overall greenspace exposure showed better working memory performance. Conclusions. These findings suggest that the cognitive benefits of greenspace exposure are context-dependent, emerging when stressors were recently present and when the need for restoration may be high. More broadly, our findings point to a dynamic, needs-based process in which everyday mobility through natural environments may support cognitive health among older adults.</jats:p>
title: Greenspace Exposure During Everyday Mobility and Working Memory in Older Adults: Momentary Benefits Amid Stressors
